theme: Google Trends tooling and datasets: pytrends, gtab anchored trends, historical trends archives, trends nowcasting repos
queries_run: gh search repos "google trends anchor" gtab --sort stars
gh search repos "google trends" nowcast --sort stars
gh search repos "trends anchor bank" --sort stars
gh search repos "google trends" travel tourism dataset --sort stars
gh search repos "google trends" historical archive --sort stars
gh search repos "google trends" airbnb OR hotel OR travel --sort stars

candidates.name: GoogleTrendsAnchorBank (gtab)
candidates.what_it_holds: Python package (MIT, EPFL DLAB, 123 stars, active as of Aug 2026) implementing the 'anchor bank' method from the WWW'20 paper 'Google Trends: The Gateway to Ranking Chart' — anchors an arbitrary set of keyword queries to a common calibrated set so relative search-interest values are comparable across time and across otherwise-unrelated pulls (fixes the resampling-noise / non-comparability problem in raw pytrends pulls). Ships as pip-installable `gtab` with example anchor banks and a CLI (`AnchorBank`, `new_query`, `set_active_gtab`).
candidates.why_useful: Directly fills gap #17 (anchored Google Trends / gtab) and speaks to gap #4 (point-in-time / comparable-magnitude series): our own note says raw Google Trends pulls are NOT point-in-time and failed as a nowcast (0/162). gtab's whole purpose is making trend magnitudes stable and comparable across separate pulls, which is the exact defect our failed test hit. Worth a controlled re-test of the ABNB/travel term set through gtab before concluding Trends is dead as a source, and it directly supports building a genuinely point-in-time trends vintage register if pulls are logged with pull dates.
candidates.size_hint: library, not a dataset; ships small example anchor-bank files

candidates.name: pytrends
candidates.what_it_holds: The canonical unofficial Google Trends Python API client (3,729 stars, updated 11 Sep 2026, custom OSS license). interest_over_time, interest_by_region, related_queries, trending_searches, realtime_trends.
candidates.why_useful: This is almost certainly the tool already behind our '9 terms, NOT point-in-time' Google Trends holding, so it is a duplicate of what we already use operationally rather than a new find — flagged for completeness and because it is the base layer several of the other candidates below (gtab, longtrends, GoogleTrends-Scraper) build on to fix the point-in-time / long-history problems pytrends alone has.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Google Trends (9 terms) already held per CONTEXT.md — pytrends is presumably the client used to pull it

candidates.name: longtrends
candidates.what_it_holds: MIT-licensed Python package (16 stars, updated 5 Jun 2026) specifically built to download and stitch together LONG-TERM Google Trends series — overlapping-window rescaling to overcome Google's short per-request lookback and resampling instability, producing one continuous multi-year daily/weekly index per keyword.
candidates.why_useful: Same problem class as gtab (comparability of Trends magnitudes over long windows) but via overlapping-window rescaling rather than anchor-bank calibration; a second, independent method to try for gap #4/#17 if gtab's anchor approach has issues, and useful for reconstructing a longer historical Trends series for travel/Airbnb-adjacent terms than our current 9-term pull.
candidates.time_coverage: as long as Google Trends itself goes back (2004+), reconstructed

candidates.name: GoogleTrends-Scraper
candidates.what_it_holds: Python implementation (226 stars, updated 2 Sep 2026) for scraping DAILY Google Trends data over long time periods by chaining overlapping weekly/monthly pulls and rescaling — same genre as longtrends, more actively maintained and higher-starred.
candidates.why_useful: Alternative, more popular long-history daily Trends reconstruction method; relevant to gap #4 (historical Trends with pull dates, if run and logged repeatedly) and gap #17 (mixed-frequency nowcasting inputs need daily rather than weekly granularity).

candidates.name: google-trends-daily
candidates.what_it_holds: GPL-3.0 Python tool (50 stars) to reconstruct daily Google Trends data over extended periods via overlapping-window stitching, one of the earlier/well-known implementations of this pattern.
candidates.why_useful: Third independent implementation of the daily-reconstruction pattern; useful as a cross-check against longtrends/GoogleTrends-Scraper outputs for the same keyword set (methodological triangulation on gap #17).

candidates.name: trendy-scraper
candidates.what_it_holds: Scrapes Google Trends data over long timescales and stitches together for daily data (75 stars, updated 10 Aug 2026) — another overlapping-window daily reconstruction tool.
candidates.why_useful: Same class as above; actively updated in 2026 which matters given Google periodically breaks the unofficial endpoints pytrends relies on.

candidates.name: adaptive-nowcasting (tourism)
candidates.what_it_holds: R repository implementing 'Adaptive Nowcasting of Tourism Statistics using Google Trends' — a method paper/code specifically for tourism-statistics nowcasting from Trends data (not consumption or GDP generically).
candidates.why_useful: Directly on-theme: a tourism-specific (not generic macro) Google-Trends nowcasting method, addressing gap #17 (mixed-frequency/nowcasting methods) with a travel-demand application closer to Airbnb nights than the generic GDP/consumption nowcasting repos below. Worth reading the method even though our own generic Trends nowcast failed — this uses an adaptive/rolling weighting scheme we have not tried.
candidates.geography: unspecified (method paper, likely a national tourism board case study)
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: overlaps failed 'Google Trends as pulled' test but is a different (adaptive) method, not yet tried

candidates.name: nowcasting-mexico
candidates.what_it_holds: Reproducible nowcasting pipeline (R + Python + Snakemake, Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20563443) for Mexican economic activity (IGAE) using Google Trends, mobility data, and Banxico (Mexican central bank) APIs; implements AR, DFM, MIDAS, LASSO, Ridge, Random Forest with pseudo out-of-sample evaluation.
candidates.why_useful: Fills gap #7 (LatAm regional travel/economic volume — Mexico specifically) via a live Banxico API client plus a full MIDAS/DFM nowcasting toolkit (also relevant to gap #17's 'nowcasting with mixed-frequency data' ask), reusable as a template even if the Google Trends leg alone is weak.
candidates.size_hint: pipeline + code, external Zenodo archive for data/results

candidates.name: google_trends_consumption_prediction
candidates.what_it_holds: 40-star repo implementing kernel-PCA-based Google Trends indicator for nowcasting US real private consumption expenditure, benchmarked against Conference Board Consumer Confidence and U. Michigan Consumer Sentiment; claims the Trends-based indicator beats both survey indices in- and out-of-sample.
candidates.why_useful: Speaks to gap #6 (consumer spend panels) via a Trends-based consumption proxy method with a published comparison against the exact survey indices (Michigan, Conference Board) already in our OECD consumer-confidence holding — a candidate cross-check even though our own generic Trends tests failed, since this targets consumption specifically via kernel PCA rather than raw levels.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: overlaps 'macro sentiment vs nights' failed test category, but untried consumption-specific PCA construction

candidates.name: gtrendsR
candidates.what_it_holds: R client for Google Trends (372 stars, updated 11 Aug 2026) — R-language equivalent of pytrends, interest-over-time/region/related-queries.
candidates.why_useful: Only relevant if the team wants an R-native Trends client (e.g. to pair with R-based nowcasting repos like adaptive-nowcasting or the Jordan BSTS repo found above); otherwise redundant with pytrends.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: functional duplicate of pytrends in a different language

candidates.name: trendspyg
candidates.what_it_holds: MIT, 50 stars, updated 12 Sep 2026 — actively maintained 'modern pytrends alternative' client (trending now, interest over time, related queries, interest by region).
candidates.why_useful: Google periodically breaks the endpoints pytrends scrapes; having a maintained alternative reduces operational risk for the weekly Trends re-pull mentioned in team memory notes. No new data, purely a resilience/tooling candidate.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: functional duplicate of pytrends, actively maintained fallback

candidates.name: trendspy
candidates.what_it_holds: MIT, 120 stars, updated 10 Sep 2026, another actively-maintained Python Google Trends client positioned as a pytrends alternative.
candidates.why_useful: Same rationale as trendspyg above — maintenance/resilience fallback, not new data.

candidates.name: pytrendsdaily
candidates.what_it_holds: MIT, 12 stars — small script specifically for fetching DAILY (not weekly) Google Trends data, built on pytrends.
candidates.why_useful: Minor/low-effort alternative for daily-granularity pulls; lower quality signal than the more-starred longtrends/GoogleTrends-Scraper repos but worth noting as another implementation of the same idea.

candidates.name: unofficial-google-trends-api
candidates.what_it_holds: 221 stars, updated 13 Aug 2026 — Python-based API using the raw HTTP Trends endpoint directly (predates/parallels pytrends).
candidates.why_useful: Another maintained fallback client if pytrends breaks; no new data.

notes: This theme is heavily saturated with pytrends forks/clones/tutorials (dozens of near-identical 1-10 star student projects re-analyzing single keyword sets) — excluded per instructions as generic ML/tutorial boilerplate. The two structurally distinct finds are (1) epfl-dlab/GoogleTrendsAnchorBank (gtab), the published anchor-bank calibration method that is the standard academic answer to the exact 'Trends magnitudes aren't comparable across pulls' problem our own 0/162 test likely ran into, and (2) a cluster of 3-4 independently-written 'long-history daily reconstruction via overlapping windows' tools (longtrends, GoogleTrends-Scraper, google-trends-daily, trendy-scraper) that could produce a longer/finer-grained Trends series than our current 9-term holding for a controlled re-test. Did not find any repo hosting a genuinely point-in-time ARCHIVE of historical Trends pulls with recorded pull-dates for travel/Airbnb terms specifically (gap #4) — everything found is a pull METHOD, not a pre-pulled point-in-time dataset; that gap looks unfilled on GitHub and would have to be built in-house by running gtab/longtrends repeatedly and logging vintages, consistent with the project's own point-in-time rule. No usable Airbnb- or hotel-specific Google Trends dataset repo was found; tourism-specific method hit was jonathanyang7/adaptive-nowcasting (R, sparse metadata, worth a closer read but not a slam dunk). Used all 6 permitted gh search calls without hitting rate limits.
